body: Paramount Closes $52 Billion Debt Financing as Century-Scale Acquisition Enters Countdown to Closing | NAI 500 English 简体中文 繁體中文 Home Articles Insights Client Press Releases Client Coverage Interviews CEO Interview PDAC Interview Clients Featured Companies In-depth Analysis Markets Stock Tracker Markets at a glance Investing 101 Investing in Mining 101 Gold and Precious Metals Electric and Battery Metals Base Metals Other Mining Subsectors METALS 100 GCFF Event Next Event Past Events Home Market News Paramount Closes $52 Billion Debt Financing as Century-Scale Acquisition Enters Countdown to Closing Paramount Closes $52 Billion Debt Financing as Century-Scale Acquisition Enters Countdown to Closing Published on: Oct 2, 2026 Author: Amy Liu Share article: Paramount has completed one of the largest media acquisitions in recent years with $52 billion in debt financing. Although financing costs have climbed and some investors are sitting on paper losses, the deal is still proceeding as planned. The combined company will span film, streaming, news, sports, and gaming, and will hold a large portfolio of super IP. However, the market will test the true value of this acquisition through actual cash flow, deleveraging progress, and content operating performance. Paramount Skydance Corporation ( PSKY )’s debt financing journey for its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery ( WBD ) reached a climax over the past week. In just one week, this film and television giant led by David Ellison crossed multiple markets and continents to sell $52 billion in loans and bonds. This cleared the way for Ellison to complete the $110 billion acquisition of Warner before October 6. As of Beijing time on October 3, the transaction was still in the pre-closing stage. The litigation settlement reached on September 21 was approved by the court on September 30, and the two sides expect to complete the acquisition on October 6. The $110 billion figure is the enterprise value including debt, while the equity value is approximately $81 billion. Financing Structure Is Complex, and the Market Experienced Repeated Twists and Turns This financing process began in February. At that time, Paramount defeated Netflix in the bidding war, and Bank of America and Citigroup, together with Apollo Global Management, provided $57.5 billion in short-term loans, constituting one of the largest bridge financings ever. From the outset, the company and its banking advisers made clear that they would simultaneously issue investment-grade bonds and junk bonds. The final financing included $30 billion in investment-grade bonds, approximately $12.4 billion in high-yield bonds, and $9.46 billion in loans. Months of preparation produced a positive return, with about 1,000 investors submitting orders. Paramount Chief Financial Officer Dennis Cinelli said the company reduced financing costs by 0.375 percentage points during the sales process, saving about $200 million in interest per year. But this caused some investors to abandon their subscriptions at the last minute, leaving those who stayed to be allocated a larger amount of debt than expected. Merger Structure Is Adjusted, and the Content Map Expands The latest changes have extended to the group’s identity and management structure. On October 2, Ellison announced that the merged parent company plans to rename itself Skydance Corporation, and that its Class B shares are expected to move to the New York Stock Exchange on October 6, with the ticker changing from “PSKY” to “SKYD.” Mattel Chief Executive Officer Ynon Kreiz will join the company and serve as co-chief executive officer after closing. The combined Paramount will hold a large portfolio of popular IP, including the Harry Potter, DC Cinematic Universe, The Matrix, The Lord of the Rings, and Dune franchises, as well as HBO’s flagship series universe. The annualized synergy target of more than $6 billion needs to be gradually converted into incremental cash. The settlement terms require the combined studio to release at least 30 theatrical films per year in the first two years, rising to 32 in the following three years.
